title: Evaluate Expression (RPN)
description:
An arithmetic expression is given by a string array A of size N. Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation.

Valid operators are +, -, *, /. Each string may be an integer or an operator.

Note: Reverse Polish Notation is equivalent to Postfix Expression, where operators are written after their operands.
story: Numbers pile up, operators combine the top two. Stack becomes a calculator that never forgets order.
plain: Reverse Polish Notation means operators come after operands. When you see a number, push it on the stack. When you see an operator, pop two numbers, apply the operator, and push the result back. The final number left on the stack is your answer. It's like doing math backwards, but the stack remembers everything for you.
tale: Imagine a tower of blocks in a dark room. You can only feel the top block. Someone calls out instructions: 'two', 'one', 'plus', 'three', 'multiply'. When you hear a number, you place a new block labeled with that number on top. When you hear 'plus' or 'multiply', you grab the top two blocks, perform the operation on their labels, and replace them with a single new block showing the result. At the end, only one block remains, glowing with the final answer. The darkness forced you to work one step at a time, but the tower never forgot what came before.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Walk through the tokens left to right. If it's a number, push it onto the stack. If it's an operator, pop two values (b then a), compute a operator b, and push the result. After processing all tokens, the stack has exactly one element—the answer.
solutions.tale: You are the tower keeper. Each token is a scroll handed to you. If the scroll has a number, you place a stone with that value on the tower. If the scroll has a plus or minus sign, you take the top two stones, combine them according to the sign's rule, and place a single new stone with the combined value. By the time the last scroll is read, only one stone stands atop the tower, holding the truth.
approach: Initialize an empty stack.
Iterate through each token in the array A.
If the token is a number, convert it to an integer and push onto the stack.
If the token is an operator (+, -, *, /), pop the top two elements (second = b, first = a).
Apply the operation: result = a operator b. Order matters for - and /.
Push the result back onto the stack.
After all tokens are processed, pop and return the final value from the stack.
This value is the evaluated result of the RPN expression.
solutions.story: Numbers stack, operators consume two and produce one. The final survivor is the answer.

title: Balanced Parenthesis
description:
Given an expression string A, examine whether the pairs and the orders of '{', '}', '(', ')', '[', ']' are correct in A.

Refer to the examples for more clarity.

Return 1 if the parenthesis sequence is balanced, else return 0.
story: Every opening bracket pushes onto the stack, every closing bracket must match the top. The stack is the memory of what's still open.
plain: Walk through the string character by character. When you see an opening bracket (like '{', '[', or '('), push it onto the stack. When you see a closing bracket, check if the stack's top matches. If it matches, pop and continue. If it doesn't match or the stack is empty, the string is unbalanced. At the end, the stack must be empty for the parentheses to be balanced.
tale: Imagine you are a doorman at a grand ballroom with three types of doors—curly, square, and round. As guests arrive, each opens one door type and you place a card for it on your desk. When a guest leaves, they must exit through the matching door, and you remove that card. If someone tries to leave through the wrong door type, or if your desk still has cards when the night ends, the building is in chaos. But if every entry has a matching exit and your desk is clear, the ballroom was perfectly balanced.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Scan the string left to right. Push every opening bracket onto the stack. When you hit a closing bracket, pop the stack and verify it's the matching opening type. If not, return 0. If you try to pop from an empty stack, return 0. After scanning, return 1 if the stack is empty, else 0.
solutions.tale: You are the gatekeeper. Each opening bracket is a guest entering, each closing bracket is a guest leaving. You write the entry type on a slip and place it atop a growing pile. When someone leaves, you check the topmost slip—does it match their exit type? If yes, tear up the slip. If no, sound the alarm. When the last guest is processed, if slips remain, the doors never fully closed. Only an empty pile means balance.
approach: Check if the string length is odd. If yes, impossible to balance—return 0 immediately.
Initialize an empty stack.
Iterate through each character in the string.
If the character is an opening bracket ('{', '[', '('), push it onto the stack.
If the character is a closing bracket ('}', ']', ')'), check if the stack is empty. If empty, return 0.
Pop the top of the stack and check if it matches the corresponding opening bracket for this closing bracket.
If mismatch, return 0. If match, continue.
After the loop, return 1 if stack is empty, else return 0.
solutions.story: Opening brackets stack up, closing brackets must match the top. Empty stack at the end means balance.

title: Min Stack
description:
Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieve the minimum element in constant time.

push(x) -- Push element x onto stack.
pop() -- Removes the element on top of the stack.
top() -- Get the top element.
getMin() -- Retrieve the minimum element in the stack.

NOTE:
All the operations have to be constant time operations.
getMin() should return -1 if the stack is empty.
pop() should return nothing if the stack is empty.
top() should return -1 if the stack is empty.
sampleInput:
push(5)
push(3)
push(7)
getMin() → 3
pop()
getMin() → 3
story: Two stacks move together. One holds values, the other holds the current minimum. Both grow and shrink in sync.
plain: Use two stacks: one for actual values, one for tracking minimums. When you push a value, also push the smaller of that value or the current minimum onto the min stack. When you pop, pop from both stacks. To get the minimum, just peek at the min stack. Both stacks stay the same size, so all operations are O(1).
tale: Imagine two towers built side by side. The left tower holds the actual numbers people give you. The right tower is your memory of 'what is the smallest number I've seen so far at each level'. Every time someone adds a number to the left, you look at the right tower's top—if the new number is smaller, you place it on the right tower too. Otherwise, you duplicate the right tower's top. When someone removes from the left, you also remove from the right. This way, the right tower always remembers the answer to 'what is the minimum right now?'

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Maintain two parallel stacks: main stack and min stack. On push, add the value to the main stack and add min(value, minStack.peek()) to the min stack. On pop, pop from both. On getMin, return minStack.peek(). All operations are O(1) since stack operations are constant time.
solutions.tale: You are a librarian managing two shelves. The left shelf holds books in the order readers return them. The right shelf holds sticky notes, each saying 'smallest book ID seen so far'. When a reader returns a book, you place it on the left shelf and write a sticky note on the right shelf with whichever is smaller: this book's ID or the current top sticky note. When a reader asks 'what's the smallest ID currently here?', you just read the top sticky note. When they check out the top book, you remove the top item from both shelves. The sticky notes are your constant-time memory.
approach: Initialize two stacks: stack (for values) and minStack (for tracking minimums).
On push(val): push val to stack. If minStack is empty, push val to minStack. Otherwise, push min(val, minStack.peek()) to minStack.
On pop(): if stack is not empty, pop from both stack and minStack.
On top(): return stack.peek() if not empty, else -1.
On getMin(): return minStack.peek() if not empty, else -1.
Both stacks have the same height at all times, so space is O(N) and all operations are O(1).
solutions.pseudocode:
stack, minStack = empty
push(val):
  stack.push(val)
  minStack.push(minStack.isEmpty() ? val : min(val, minStack.peek()))
pop():
  if !stack.isEmpty(): stack.pop(); minStack.pop()
getMin():
  return minStack.isEmpty() ? -1 : minStack.peek()
solutions.story: Main stack holds values. Min stack mirrors it, always keeping the current minimum at the top. Both rise and fall together.

title: Redundant Braces
description:
Given a string A denoting an expression. It contains the following operators '+', '-', '*', '/'.

Check whether A has redundant braces or not.

NOTE: A will be always a valid expression and will not contain any white spaces.

Return 1 if A has redundant braces else return 0.
story: Push everything until you hit a closing bracket. Then unwind—if you never saw an operator, those brackets were useless.
plain: Scan the expression left to right, pushing every character onto a stack. When you hit a closing parenthesis, pop characters until you reach the matching opening parenthesis. If you popped at least one operator (+, -, *, /) during that process, the brackets were necessary. If you didn't pop any operator, the brackets were redundant. Return 1 if redundant brackets are found, 0 otherwise.
tale: Imagine you are a clerk reading a scroll of instructions. Each symbol goes into a box. When you see a closing parenthesis, you empty the box back to the matching opening parenthesis, counting what you see. If you empty the box and never saw a plus, minus, multiply, or divide sign, those parentheses held nothing but a naked value—they were decorative,not functional. Sound the alarm. But if you saw at least one operator, those parentheses were doing real work.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Iterate through the string. Push every character onto the stack. When you encounter a closing bracket ')', start popping and check if you popped at least one operator before hitting '('. If no operator was popped, return 1 (redundant). If you finish the string without finding redundancy, return 0.
solutions.tale: You are a quality inspector for mathematical expressions. Each symbol is a worker entering a room. When a closing bracket arrives, you call out everyone who entered after the last opening bracket. If among those workers there's at least one operator (a plus, minus, multiply, or divide worker), the brackets earned their keep. But if you only see letter workers (variables), the brackets were redundant—just wrapping a value with no computation. You stamp 'redundant' and return 1.
approach: Initialize an empty stack.
Iterate through each character in the expression string A.
If the character is ')', it's a closing bracket—time to check.
Pop characters from the stack until you hit '('.
While popping, track if you saw at least one operator (+, -, *, /).
If you didn't see any operator, return 1 (redundant brackets found).
Otherwise, continue iterating.
If the loop completes without finding redundancy, return 0.
solutions.story: Push characters. On ')', unwind to '(' and count operators. No operator seen means redundant brackets.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description:
Given an array of integers A representing heights of histogram bars where the width of each bar is 1, find the area of the largest rectangle formed by the histogram.

A represents a histogram i.e A[i] denotes the height of the ith histogram's bar. Width of each bar is 1.
story: For each bar, find how far left and right it can extend as the shortest. Width × height = area. Stack finds boundaries in linear time.
plain: For each bar at index i, we need to find the maximum width rectangle where that bar is the shortest. To do this, find the nearest smaller bar to the left and right. The width is the distance between those boundaries. Use a monotonic stack to compute nearest smaller elements in O(N) time for both directions, then calculate area for each bar and return the maximum.
tale: Imagine a city skyline where each building can expand its footprint left and right until it hits a shorter building. A tower at height 5 looks left and right: 'How far can I stretch before I meet someone shorter than me?' The answer is the widest rectangle I can claim. You walk the skyline twice with a memory tablet (the stack), once left-to-right recording 'who is your left boundary?', once right-to-left recording 'who is your right boundary?' Then each tower multiplies its height by its width and proclaims its area. The loudest voice wins.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Compute two arrays using monotonic stacks: prevSmaller[i] (index of nearest smaller to left, or -1) and nextSmaller[i] (index of nearest smaller to right, or N). For each bar i, the width it can extend is nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i] - 1. Calculate area[i] = height[i] × width[i] for all bars and return the maximum.
solutions.tale: You are a land surveyor with a magical compass. First pass: walk left to right, and for each bar, the compass points to the last shorter bar you saw (or the edge). Record those indices. Second pass: walk right to left, same rule. Now each bar knows its left and right boundaries. Compute each bar's rectangular footprint. The largest footprint is the answer. The compass is the stack—it only remembers bars in increasing order, discarding taller ones when a shorter arrives.
approach: Compute prevSmaller[i] for each i: index of nearest smaller element to the left (or -1 if none).
Compute nextSmaller[i] for each i: index of nearest smaller element to the right (or N if none).
Both computed using monotonic increasing stack in O(N) each.
For each bar i, calculate width = nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i] - 1.
Calculate area = A[i] × width.
Track the maximum area across all bars.
Return the maximum area.
The stack-based NSE computation is the key insight that reduces brute force O(N²) to O(N).
solutions.pseudocode:
prevSmaller = nearestSmallerLeft(A)  // O(N)
nextSmaller = nearestSmallerRight(A) // O(N)
maxArea = 0
for i in 0..N-1:
  width = nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i] - 1
  area = A[i] * width
  maxArea = max(maxArea, area)
return maxArea
solutions.story: Find left and right boundaries using stack, then width × height for each bar. Maximum is the answer.

title: Nearest Smaller Element
description:
Given an array A, find the nearest smaller element G[i] for every element A[i] in the array such that the element has an index smaller than i.

More formally,
G[i] for an element A[i] = an element A[j] such that
j is maximum possible AND
j < i AND
A[j] < A[i]

Elements for which no smaller element exist, consider the next smaller element as -1.
story: Maintain a stack of increasing values. When you see a new value, pop all larger ones—they'll never be nearest smaller for anyone. The remaining top is your answer.
plain: Scan the array left to right. Keep a stack that holds values in increasing order. For each element, pop stack elements that are greater than or equal to the current element (they can't be the nearest smaller for this element). If the stack is empty after popping, there's no smaller element to the left, so record -1. Otherwise, the stack top is the nearest smaller. Then push the current element onto the stack.
tale: You walk through a line of guards, each with a height. You're looking for each guard's 'protector'—the nearest shorter guard to their left. You carry a list (the stack) of guards you've seen so far, sorted shortest to tallest. When you meet a new guard, you remove anyone from your list who is taller or equal height—they're blocked by this new guard and will never protect anyone ahead. The shortest person left on your list is the protector. If the list is empty, this guard has no protector. Add the new guard to your list and continue.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Iterate left to right. Maintain a monotonic increasing stack (stores values, not indices). For each A[i], pop while stack.peek() >= A[i]. If stack is empty, record -1. Else record stack.peek(). Push A[i]. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so O(N) total.
solutions.tale: Imagine a tower of blocks stacked smallest to largest. As you walk through numbers, you place each new number on the tower. But first, you knock off any blocks that are equal or taller than the incoming number—they're now useless. What remains on top is the nearest smaller. If the tower is empty, no one is smaller. The tower only grows with useful candidates, keeping the operation fast.
approach: Initialize an empty stack and an empty result array of size N.
Set result[0] = -1 (no element before index 0). Push A[0] onto the stack.
For i = 1 to N-1:
Pop from stack while stack.peek() >= A[i]. If stack becomes empty, set result[i] = -1.
If stack is not empty, set result[i] = stack.peek().
Push A[i] onto the stack.
Return the result array.
Each element is pushed once and popped once, giving O(N) time.
solutions.pseudocode:
stack = empty
res[0] = -1; stack.push(A[0])
for i = 1 to N-1:
  while !stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() >= A[i]:
    stack.pop()
  res[i] = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek()
  stack.push(A[i])
return res

title: Double Character Trouble
description:
You have a string, denoted as A.

To transform the string, you should perform the following operation repeatedly:
Identify the first occurrence of consecutive identical pairs of characters within the string.
Remove this pair of identical characters from the string.
Repeat steps 1 and 2 until there are no more consecutive identical pairs of characters.

The final result will be the transformed string.
story: Stack eliminates consecutive duplicates. Push if different from top, pop if same. What remains is the cleansed string.
plain: Scan the string left to right. Maintain a stack of characters. For each character, if the stack is empty or the top is different, push the character. If the top matches the current character, pop (they cancel out). After processing all characters, pop the stack into a string to get the result. The stack automatically removes all consecutive identical pairs.
tale: Imagine you're stacking letter tiles on a table. Each time you pick a new tile, you compare it to the top of your stack. If they're the same letter, you throw both away—they annihilate like matter and antimatter. If they're different, you place the new tile on the stack. By the time you finish, only tiles that survived the annihilation remain, forming the final word.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Iterate through the string. If the stack is empty, push the character. If the stack's top equals the current character, pop (remove the pair). Otherwise, push the current character. After processing, convert the stack to a string by popping elements and building in reverse order. This gives the final result.
solutions.tale: You are a librarian sorting books with a simple rule: if two identical books sit next to each other, they vanish. You walk down the aisle, checking each book against the top of your current pile. Same title? Both disappear. Different title? Add the new book to the pile. At the end, only the unpaired books remain, forming the cleaned collection.

Iterate through each character in the string A.
If the stack is empty, push the character.
If the stack is not empty and the top element equals the current character, pop the stack (pair found and removed).
Otherwise, push the current character onto the stack.
After the loop, build the result string by popping all characters from the stack and prepending them (reverse order).
Return the result string.
Each character is pushed and potentially popped once, giving O(N) time.

title: Passing Game
description:
There is a football event going on in your city. In this event, you are given A passes and players having ids between 1 and 10⁶.

Initially, some player with a given id had the ball in his possession. You have to make a program to display the id of the player who possessed the ball after exactly A passes.

There are two kinds of passes:
1) ID
2) 0

For the first kind of pass, the player in possession of the ball passes the ball "forward" to the player with id = ID.
For the second kind of pass, the player in possession of the ball passes the ball back to the player who had forwarded the ball to him.

In the second kind of pass "0" just means Back Pass.
Return the ID of the player who currently possesses the ball.
story: Forward pass pushes new player to stack. Back pass (0) pops current, reveals previous. Stack tracks possession chain.
plain: Start with the initial player B on the stack. Process each pass in array C. If C[i] is a player ID (not 0), it's a forward pass—push that player ID onto the stack. If C[i] is 0, it's a back pass—pop the stack to remove the current player, and the new top is who now has the ball. After all A passes, return the top of the stack (current ball holder).
tale: Imagine a chain of football players passing a ball. You keep a notebook (the stack) listing who currently holds the ball and who passed to them. When player X passes forward to player Y, you write Y's name on a new page on top. When someone shouts 'back pass!', you tear off the top page—the ball returns to the player whose name is now visible. After all passes, the top page shows the final ball holder.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Initialize a stack and push the starting player B. Iterate through the A passes. For each pass, if C[i] != 0, push C[i] (forward pass). If C[i] == 0, pop the stack (back pass). After processing all passes, return stack.peek() (current ball holder). The stack naturally tracks the chain of possession.
solutions.tale: You are the referee with a clipboard. You write down the starting player. For each pass: if it's a forward pass to a new player, add their name to the list. If it's a back pass, cross out the current name and go back to the previous one. At the final whistle, the last name on your clipboard is the answer.
approach: Initialize a stack and push the starting player ID (B).
Set currentPlayer = B.
Iterate through each pass i from 0 to A-1:
If C[i] == 0 (back pass): pop the stack, then set currentPlayer = stack.peek() (previous player).
If C[i] != 0 (forward pass): set currentPlayer = C[i], then push C[i] onto the stack.
After all passes are processed, return currentPlayer (or stack.peek()).
Each pass is O(1), giving O(A) total time.
solutions.pseudocode:
stack = empty
stack.push(B)
currentPlayer = B
for i = 0 to A-1:
  if C[i] == 0:
    stack.pop()
    currentPlayer = stack.peek()
  else:
    currentPlayer = C[i]
    stack.push(C[i])
return currentPlayer
solutions.story: Stack simulates possession chain. Forward pass → push. Back pass (0) → pop, peek. O(A) time.

title: Check Two Bracket Expressions
description:
Given two strings A and B. Each string represents an expression consisting of lowercase English alphabets, '+', '-', '(' and ')'.

The task is to compare them and check if they are similar. If they are identical, return 1 else return 0.

NOTE: It may be assumed that there are at most 26 operands from 'a' to 'z', and every operand appears only once.
story: Track cumulative sign for each variable through nested brackets. Two expressions are identical if all variables have the same effective sign.
plain: Walk through each expression and track the effective sign of each variable (a-z) considering nested brackets. Use a stack to remember the cumulative sign at each bracket level. When you enter a bracket, push the inherited sign. When you exit, pop. Record each variable's final sign. Compare sign arrays—if identical, the expressions are equivalent.
tale: Imagine two scribes writing equations in different handwriting. You decode each scribe's work by walking through their symbols with a memory tablet (the stack). The tablet remembers 'am I in a positive or negative context?' When a bracket opens, you write down the new context. When it closes, you erase that layer. Each letter gets stamped with its final sign. If both scribes' stamps match for all 26 letters, their equations say the same thing, just differently dressed.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Parse both expressions using a stack-based sign tracker. For each character: '+' sets current sign to +1, '-' sets it to -1, '(' pushes the inherited context onto the stack, ')' pops it, and a-z records the effective sign (stack.peek() × currentSign). After parsing both, compare the 26-element sign arrays. If all match, return 1. Otherwise, return 0.
solutions.tale: You are a sign detective. For each expression, you carry a stack of context clues—'are we inside a negated region?' As you read symbols, you note each letter's true sign by multiplying the stack's top context with the immediate sign. Opening brackets inherit and deepen context; closing brackets lighten it. At the end, you compare your two sign tables. If they match letter-by-letter, the expressions are twins.
approach: Initialize a sign array of size 26 for each expression (one per letter a-z).
Use a stack to track cumulative sign context. Start with stack containing +1 (positive context).
Set currentSign = 1 (positive by default).
For each character: if '+', set currentSign = 1; if '-', set currentSign = -1.
If '(', push stack.peek() × currentSign onto stack (inherit outer sign), then reset currentSign = 1.
If ')', pop the stack (exit bracket context).
If a-z, record sign[char - 'a'] = stack.peek() × currentSign.
After parsing both expressions, compare their sign arrays element by element.
If all 26 elements match, return 1. Otherwise, return 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
signA = parseSigns(A)
signB = parseSigns(B)
for i = 0 to 25:
  if signA[i] != signB[i]: return 0
return 1

parseSigns(expr):
  sign[26] = 0
  stack = [1]
  currentSign = 1
  for c in expr:
    if c == '+': currentSign = 1
    elif c == '-': currentSign = -1
    elif c == '(': stack.push(stack.peek() * currentSign); currentSign = 1
    elif c == ')': stack.pop()
    else: sign[c-'a'] = stack.peek() * currentSign
  return sign
solutions.story: Parse both expressions with sign-tracking stack. Compare 26-element sign arrays. Match → 1, mismatch → 0.

title: Infix to Postfix
description:
Given string A denoting an infix expression. Convert the infix expression into a postfix expression.

String A consists of ^, /, *, +, -, (, ) and lowercase English alphabets where lowercase English alphabets are operands and ^, /, *, +, - are operators.

Find and return the postfix expression of A.

NOTE:
^ has the highest precedence.
/ and * have equal precedence but greater than + and -.
+ and - have equal precedence and lowest precedence among given operators.
story: Operands go straight to output. Operators wait on a stack, popped by higher precedence. Brackets create walls that operators can't cross.
plain: Scan the infix expression left to right. Operands (letters/digits) go directly to the output. When you see an operator, pop from the stack all operators with greater or equal precedence and append them to output, then push the current operator. Opening brackets push as walls. Closing brackets pop everything until the matching opening bracket. After scanning, pop remaining operators. The result is the postfix expression.
tale: Imagine a conveyor belt carrying symbols. Operands slide straight into the output box. Operators wait in a tower (the stack), but only if they're stronger than the one on top—weaker operators must wait for their turn and get ejected first. Parentheses are magic doors: opening doors create a sealed room where operators hide, and closing doors flush everyone out of that room. By the end, the tower is empty and the output box holds the reordered expression.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Iterate through the string. If the character is an operand, append to output. If it's '(', push to stack. If it's ')', pop and append until '(' is found, then discard '('. If it's an operator, pop all operators from stack with precedence >= current operator's precedence (but don't pop past '('), then push current operator. After the loop, pop all remaining operators. Return the output string.
solutions.tale: You are a train conductor rerouting cargo. Letters (operands) go straight to the destination. Symbols (operators) wait at a station (stack) sorted by priority. When a new operator arrives, all operators with equal or higher priority must leave first—they go to the destination. Opening brackets build a wall at the station; closing brackets tear it down, sending everyone behind the wall to the destination. At journey's end, all operators at the station board the final train.
approach: Initialize an empty stack and an empty output string.
Iterate through each character in the infix expression.
If the character is a letter or digit (operand), append it to the output.
If the character is '(', push it onto the stack.
If the character is ')', pop from stack and append to output until '(' is encountered. Discard '('.
If the character is an operator, pop from stack while: stack is not empty AND top != '(' AND precedence(top) >= precedence(current). Append popped operators to output. Then push the current operator.
After the loop, pop all remaining operators from the stack and append to output.
Return the output string.
Precedence: ^ = 3, * and / = 2, + and - = 1.
solutions.story: Operands → output. Operators → stack (pop >= precedence first). '(' → wall. ')' → flush until '('. O(N) time.

title: MAX and MIN
description:
Given an array of integers A.

The value of an array is computed as the difference between the maximum element in the array and the minimum element in the array A.

Calculate and return the sum of values of all possible subarrays of A modulo 10⁹+7.
story: Each element contributes as MAX in some subarrays and MIN in others. Count both contributions using monotonic stacks.
plain: For each element, count how many subarrays have it as the maximum (it contributes positively) and how many have it as the minimum (it contributes negatively). Use four arrays computed via monotonic stacks: prevSmaller, nextSmaller (to count MIN contributions), prevGreater, nextGreater (to count MAX contributions). For element i, its contribution = A[i] × (count as MAX) - A[i] × (count as MIN). Sum all contributions modulo 10⁹+7.
tale: Imagine each number in the array is a village elder with a height. You ask each elder: 'In how many village gatherings are you the tallest?' and 'In how many are you the shortest?' The answer depends on how far left and right they can see before hitting someone taller or shorter. You use four compass readings (the stacks) to find these boundaries quickly. Each elder's pride (positive contribution) minus their humility (negative contribution) is tallied. The sum of all egos is the answer.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Compute four arrays: prevSmaller[i] (index of nearest smaller to left, or -1), nextSmaller[i] (index of nearest smaller to right, or N), prevGreater[i] (index of nearest greater to left, or -1), nextGreater[i] (index of nearest greater to right, or N). All computed in O(N) using monotonic stacks. For each element i, count as MAX = (i - prevGreater[i]) × (nextGreater[i] - i), count as MIN = (i - prevSmaller[i]) × (nextSmaller[i] - i). Contribution[i] = A[i] × countAsMax - A[i] × countAsMin. Sum all contributions modulo 10⁹+7.
solutions.tale: You are an accountant for a kingdom where each number is a merchant. Each merchant trades in multiple markets (subarrays). In some markets they're the richest (maximum), in others the poorest (minimum). You hire four scouts with telescopes (the stacks) to find how many markets each merchant dominates or trails in. For each merchant, you credit their wealth times their dominance count, and debit their wealth times their trailing count. The kingdom's total balance is the sum of all ledgers.
approach: Compute prevSmaller[i] for all i using monotonic increasing stack (left to right).
Compute nextSmaller[i] for all i using monotonic increasing stack (right to left).
Compute prevGreater[i] for all i using monotonic decreasing stack (left to right).
Compute nextGreater[i] for all i using monotonic decreasing stack (right to left).
For each element i:
countAsMax = (i - prevGreater[i]) × (nextGreater[i] - i) — subarrays where A[i] is maximum.
countAsMin = (i - prevSmaller[i]) × (nextSmaller[i] - i) — subarrays where A[i] is minimum.
contribution[i] = A[i] × countAsMax - A[i] × countAsMin.
Sum all contributions modulo 10⁹+7 and return.
solutions.pseudocode:
prevSmaller = computePrevSmaller(A)
nextSmaller = computeNextSmaller(A)
prevGreater = computePrevGreater(A)
nextGreater = computeNextGreater(A)
sum = 0
for i = 0 to N-1:
  countMax = (i - prevGreater[i]) * (nextGreater[i] - i)
  countMin = (i - prevSmaller[i]) * (nextSmaller[i] - i)
  sum += A[i] * countMax - A[i] * countMin
  sum %= MOD
return sum

title: Max Rectangle in Binary Matrix
description:
Given a 2-D binary matrix A of size N x M filled with 0's and 1's, find the largest rectangle containing only ones and return its area.

Note: Rows are numbered from top to bottom and columns are numbered from left to right.
story: Treat each row as the base of a histogram. Heights = consecutive 1s above. Run largest rectangle in histogram for each row.
plain: Convert the matrix into histograms row by row. For each row, compute a height array where height[j] is the number of consecutive 1s from the current row upwards in column j. If the current cell is 0, height[j] resets to 0. For each row's height array, apply the largest rectangle in histogram algorithm using stacks. Track the maximum area across all rows.
tale: Imagine a city where each row is a street level, and buildings are columns of stacked ones. You walk down the city, floor by floor. At each floor, you measure how tall each column of ones has grown from the ground to this floor. If a zero appears, that column crumbles to zero height. On each floor, you run the 'largest rectangle in histogram' spell to find the widest rooftop rectangle of buildings at that level. The best rooftop across all floors is your answer.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Initialize a height array of size M (columns). Iterate through each row. For each column j, if A[i][j] == 1, increment height[j], else reset height[j] = 0. After updating heights for row i, run largestRectangleInHistogram(height) to get the max area rectangle with row i as the base. Track the overall maximum across all rows. The largestRectangleInHistogram function uses stacks to find nearest smaller elements in O(M) time.
solutions.tale: You are an architect with a blueprint of a binary city. You walk down each floor. On each floor, you update your height map—each column's tower grows if it's a 1, collapses if it's a 0. After updating, you call your assistant (the histogram algorithm) to find the largest rectangle that can be drawn using those tower heights. Your assistant uses a magic stack to solve it instantly. You record the best rectangle found on any floor. By the time you reach the basement, you have the largest rectangular area in the entire city.
approach: Initialize height array of size M (number of columns), all zeros.
Iterate through each row i from 0 to N-1:
For each column j:
If A[i][j] == 1, increment height[j] by 1 (extend the tower).
If A[i][j] == 0, set height[j] = 0 (tower collapses).
After updating heights for row i, compute maxArea for this histogram using largestRectangleInHistogram(height).
Track the maximum area across all rows.
Return the maximum area.
largestRectangleInHistogram uses stacks to find prevSmaller and nextSmaller in O(M).
solutions.story: Row-by-row histogram. Update heights (1 → grow, 0 → collapse). Run histogram area for each row. Track max. O(N×M).

title: Next Greater Element
description:
Given an array A, find the next greater element G[i] for every element A[i] in the array.

The next greater element for an element A[i] is the first greater element on the right side of A[i] in the array, A.

More formally:
G[i] for an element A[i] = an element A[j] such that
j is minimum possible AND
j > i AND
A[j] > A[i]

Elements for which no greater element exists, consider the next greater element as -1.
story: Scan right to left with a monotonic decreasing stack. Pop smaller or equal elements—they're blocked. The remaining top is the next greater.
plain: Traverse the array from right to left. Maintain a stack that holds values in decreasing order. For each element, pop stack values that are less than or equal to the current element (they can't be next greater). If the stack is empty, no greater element exists (record -1). Otherwise, the stack top is the next greater. Push the current element onto the stack. This ensures each element is processed once, giving O(N) time.
tale: Imagine you're walking backwards through a line of sentries, each with a height. For each sentry, you ask: 'Who is the next taller sentry ahead of me?' You keep a memory list (the stack) of sentries ahead, sorted tallest at bottom. When you meet a new sentry, you discard anyone on your list who is shorter or equal—this new sentry blocks them. Whoever remains on top of your list is the next taller. If the list is empty, no one ahead is taller. Add the new sentry to your list and step back.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Iterate right to left. Maintain a monotonic decreasing stack (stores values). For each A[i], pop while stack.peek() <= A[i]. If stack is empty, record -1. Else record stack.peek(). Push A[i]. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so O(N) total.
solutions.tale: You walk backwards through a row of towers, noting the next taller tower ahead of each. You carry a list of towers behind you, kept in descending order. When you reach a new tower, you remove any tower from your list that this new tower blocks (shorter or equal). The tallest remaining tower on your list is the answer. If your list is empty, no tower ahead is taller. The list only keeps useful candidates, so the walk is fast.
approach: Initialize an empty stack and a result array of size N.
Set result[N-1] = -1 (no element after the last). Push A[N-1] onto the stack.
For i = N-2 down to 0:
Pop from stack while stack.peek() <= A[i]. If stack becomes empty, set result[i] = -1.
If stack is not empty, set result[i] = stack.peek().
Push A[i] onto the stack.
Return the result array.
Each element is pushed once and popped once, giving O(N) time.
solutions.pseudocode:
stack = empty
res[N-1] = -1; stack.push(A[N-1])
for i = N-2 downto 0:
  while !stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() <= A[i]:
    stack.pop()
  res[i] = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek()
  stack.push(A[i])
return res
solutions.story: Monotonic decreasing stack. Pop all <= current, remaining top is next greater. Push current. O(N) time.

title: Sort Stack Using Another Stack
description:
Given a stack of integers A, sort it using another stack.

Return the array of integers after sorting the stack using another stack.
story: Transfer elements from input to sorted stack. If top of sorted is larger, move it back temporarily. Repeat until input is empty.
plain: Use two stacks: input (original) and sorted (auxiliary). While input is not empty, pop an element. If sorted is empty or sorted's top is less than or equal to the element, push the element onto sorted. Otherwise, pop elements from sorted back to input until you find the right position, then push the element onto sorted. After all elements are transferred, sorted holds the elements in ascending order (smallest at bottom, largest at top). Convert to array.
tale: Imagine you have two towers of blocks. The left tower (input) is messy. The right tower (sorted) will be perfectly stacked, smallest at bottom. You take the top block from the left. If the right tower's top is smaller or empty, place your block on it. But if the right tower's top is bigger, you must temporarily move those bigger blocks back to the left until you find where your block fits. This dance continues until the left tower is empty and the right tower is sorted.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Pop elements from input one by one. For each element, compare with sorted's top. If sorted is empty or sorted.peek() <= element, push element onto sorted. Otherwise, pop from sorted and push back to input until you find the correct position (or sorted becomes empty), then push element onto sorted. Continue until input is empty. Finally, pop all from sorted into a result array (largest to smallest), then reverse to get ascending order.
solutions.tale: You are organizing a deck of cards using two piles. The left pile is shuffled, the right pile will be sorted (bottom = smallest). Pick a card from the left. If the right pile's top card is smaller or the pile is empty, place your card on the right. If the right pile's top is larger, move those large cards back to the left pile until your card fits. Once the left pile is empty, the right pile is sorted. Flip it over for ascending order.
approach: Push all elements of input array into stack 'input'.
Initialize empty stack 'sorted'.
While input is not empty:
Pop an element 'x' from input.
While sorted is not empty AND sorted.peek() > x:
Pop from sorted and push back to input (make room for x).
Push x onto sorted.
After the loop, sorted contains elements in ascending order (top = largest).
Pop all elements from sorted into a result array (this gives largest to smallest).
Reverse the result array to get ascending order (or pop into array from index N-1 to 0).
Return the result array.
solutions.story: Transfer from input to sorted, moving larger elements back temporarily. O(N²) time, O(N) space.
